print('\\n'.join(parts[:3]))

strengths: MaskSub offers a useful, technically coherent training improvement: a masked forward pass learns from stopped-gradient predictions of the unmasked pass, with shared weights and unchanged inference architecture. The supported practical contribution provides a stronger case for acceptance than rejection.

Improvements persist across strong training recipes and model scales. Table 1 reports gains of 0.3–0.7 percentage points across ViT-S/B/L/H and both training lengths. Tables 3 and 5 extend the evidence to pretrained models, ResNets, and Swin Transformers, generally using a fixed 50% masking ratio.

The training-budget comparisons substantiate practical efficiency. Table 7 reports 84.1% for ViT-B with MaskSub versus 83.7% for longer baseline training at approximately equal cost. Table 8 also shows higher accuracy than CoSub, 84.1% versus 83.9%, using 25.1 versus 35.3 GPU-days.

The appendix establishes relevance beyond ImageNet classification. MaskSub pretraining improves ADE20K segmentation by 0.4–0.6 mIoU, COCO detection and instance segmentation by 0.2 and 0.3 AP, respectively, and multiple distribution-shift benchmarks. ImageNet-A gains are particularly substantial, including 36.8% to 41.9% for ViT-B.

The ablations support the design choices. Table A.6 shows substantially smaller gains without the distillation loss; Tables A.7–A.8 examine masking ratios and loss weights. Repeated-run results strengthen the central evidence: Table A.12 reports ViT-B accuracy of 83.46±0.04 versus 84.08±0.02. Algorithm 1, detailed training tables, and the supplied code link support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual originality is moderate: the method combines established self-distillation and augmentation consistency with MAE-style token removal. Its distinction from related submodel methods is principally the asymmetric masking configuration and demonstrated usefulness. Moreover, Table 6 compares competing self-distillation methods under weaker training recipes, so it does not establish the claimed incompatibility of those methods with modern recipes such as RSB.

The explanation of 'automatic difficulty control' exceeds the evidence. Equation (3) supervises every masked example, and its gradient depends on prediction disagreement rather than teacher correctness. Figure 3's aggregate gradient norms therefore do not establish that masking is effectively restricted to successfully learned examples. Figure 2 also measures convergence per epoch despite additional computation per epoch.

The benefits have meaningful limits. Table A.9 shows that adding MaskSub during ViT-B finetuning reduces CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.69% to 89.55%, and Section 4.2 states that peak CLIP finetuning accuracy matches the baseline. ResNet and Swin implementations require approximately twice the training computation because masked tokens cannot be removed. These results qualify the broad claims of consistently beneficial, inexpensive regularization.

Statistical support is uneven. Although several experiments include three-run statistics, uncertainty is absent for the 0.1-point BEiT v2 improvements and small COCO gains. Their reliability is less established than the central ViT training results, and blanket claims of significant improvements are too strong.

There are correctable reporting errors: Table 10 lists the ViT-S Cars improvement from 80.9% to 92.2% as +1.3 rather than +11.3 points. Section 4.4 claims one-sixth of GradAug's finetuning cost, whereas Table 9 reports 8.6 versus 23.4 GPU-days, approximately 37%. These are presentation issues rather than fundamental flaws in the method.
